newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: City of Prague to decide foreign debt issue Thurs.
newsitem.headline: City of Prague to decide foreign debt issue Thurs.

text.p: Final approval for a $300 million City of Prague five or seven year international bond issue will be decided by the full City Council on Thursday, a spokeswoman for city hall told Reuters on Wednesday.

"The (executive) council has approved it and will face the Prague representative (council) with a proposal for obtaining foreign-source funds in the amount of $300 million," Michaela Kynkorova told Reuters.
"(The issue would be) in the form of a bond issue of the City of Prague on international financial markets... it has not yet been determined which... with maturity in five or seven years."
She said the bond was expected to carry a coupon of around seven percent, with a launch date in possibly September or October.
The city executive has been planning a debt issue for months, but in the past has cited market conditions for delaying a final decision.
A meeting of the full representative council is set for 9 a.m. local time (0700 gmt).

The plan, to raise funds for transport infrastructure projects, has come under fire from central bank and government officials who complain that the issue would exacerbate Czech macroeconomic problems by bringing more funds into circulation.
"The leadership of the city is consulting with the (Czech National Bank) about the issue... and the CNB is informed about how the issue plans are progressing via Mayor (Jan) Koukal," Kynkorova said.
Prague carries an indicative investment-grade "A" rating from Standard & Poor's, the same as the Czech sovereign debt.
Kynkorova said that an arranger for the issue would be chosen by a public tender.
The city's plan in 1995 for a 20-year Japanese placement was criticised by the Czech National Bank (CNB), and the issue was never launched.

The Czech economy was shaken in late May by a speculative attack on the crown which forced the central bank to float the currency and it fell to more than 15 percent below its highs against the dollar and mark in early February.

The controlled float of the currency was backed by a rise in key interest rates and a government austerity package meant to slow domestic demand and keep the inflationary effects of the crown's depreciation in check.
